name: Suparinpei
description: The most comprehensive kata in Goju-Ryu with 108 techniques and movements.

origin.title: Origin
origin.content: Suparinpei is very old in origin. According to tradition, Higaonna's student Chōjun Miyagi inherited it from Ryu Ryu Ko's system as "Pechurin" (a romanization for 108) and later modernized it to Suparinpei. According to some stories, the name refers to Yue Fei's 108 gripping techniques (108 Seizing & Grabbing). The kata is comparable to traditional Chinese forms of Shaolin, Tiger or Crane. Within the goju community, it is assumed that Miyagi learned the kata from Higaonna or during self-study in China. In fact, the kata has had no namesake found in Okinawa; it is simply the most comprehensive form from the Goju arsenal.

transmission.title: Transmission to Goju-Ryu
transmission.content: The transmission goes via the Higaonna→Miyagi line. Chōjun Miyagi undoubtedly preserved Suparinpei as the last kata in the system. In To'on-Ryū (Kyoda) and Shito-Ryū, versions of this kata also appear, which indicates that Higaonna may have shared it with his students. In the Goju tradition, Suparinpei remained limited to the highest grades (black belt).

historicalDevelopment.title: Historical Development
historicalDevelopment.content: Suparinpei has never been shortened over the years; it remains the longest Goju kata (typically 108+ movements). There are some interpretation differences (direction of turns, breathing rhythms) but generally the kata has been consistently preserved from Miyagi's generation. It formerly had the Okinawan name "Pechurin" and is still called that in some circles. Mas Oyama called it "Hangetsu" in Kyokushin (like in Shotokan) – same as Seisan – but that is a name change for a Shorin version. Within Goju it remains Suparinpei.

technicalFeatures.title: Technical and Philosophical Characteristics
technicalFeatures.content: Suparinpei contains literally everything that Goju-Ryu has: hard and soft strikes, various kicks (including double lateral/horizontal) and extensive lock and throw techniques. The kata arranges movements from all previous kata (hence the number 108). Bunkai is legion: from openings for punches to complex throws. The kata strengthens the entire body and endurance and serves as the pinnacle of the Goju principle (especially jin, the mirroring of attack with energy). Breathing and tension vary: as in Tensho and Sanchin, both hard and soft breathing occur. A well-known philosophy is that whoever masters Suparinpei has learned the essence of Karate (hence the association with "nirvana" in ancient traditions).

controversy.title: Controversy/Variations within Goju-Ryu
controversy.content: There is no real controversy; Suparinpei is so complex that everyone mainly struggles with their own version. Sometimes there are small differences between Okinawa and Japan (how strictly the hachiji dachi is used, for example). The main "variation" lies in interpretation (where each other's line sometimes recognizes unusual grips). There are indications that Kyoda's Tōon-ryū also knows it under the name "Kururunfa" for the last part, but that is speculative.

relationships.title: Relationship to Other Kata/Systems
relationships.content: Suparinpei is the ultimate kata in Goju-ryu and has parallels in other Okinawan systems (the Eagle Claw Yī Bǎi Líng Bā Qín Ná, 108 grips of General Yue Fei, or the Shaolin "Fu Zhen" kata). Funakoshi's Hangetsu kata for Shotokan is actually a highly streamlined version of (part of) Suparinpei/Seisan. In Kyokushin, some schools also teach a form with 108 movements, which underscores the historical kinship. Essentially, Suparinpei connects Goju-Ryu back to traditional Chinese Kung Fu systems through the number 108 and the integral combination of techniques.

modernPractice.title: Use in Modern Practice
modernPractice.content: In Goju dojos, Suparinpei is reserved for the highest grades. It is rarely done in competition (too long and too specific), but practiced for theory and conditioning. In contemporary lessons, Suparinpei serves as a test case for comprehension: students often analyze the bunkai to extract all possible attacks/defenses. In self-defense context, it is mainly a demonstration of the 'round' final attack (often with two short diagonal kicks and closing open hand). It is not a form that one practices casually; whoever masters Suparinpei completes the karate program.

nameAndMeaning.title: Name and Meaning
nameAndMeaning.content: Suparinpei means "108 hands/techniques". The Japanese name is built from (100), (100), (0), (8) and (hand) – which together indicates 108. In Chinese, the kata had a different name ("Pechurin" or similar) which may indicate a homonym. 108 is a sacred Buddhist number (think of the 108 powers of Yue Fei's Eagle Claw). Sometimes Suparinpei is translated as "108 steps", but actually it's about the number 108 in the kata.
